  • First with one model, sixteenth with another

    Nov 17, 2026

    Runta and Baseten ran 27,280 agent trials — 22 harness configurations across 5 open models — and measured what harness leaderboards were hiding: with the model fixed, the harness moves cost per task 1.8 to 5.0x, and the most expensive harness per pass usually passed less often than the cheapest. The same shape runs through accuracy: Wiz's arena shows a 5.1-point mean gap for the same models across two harnesses, and ARC-AGI-3's Standard-versus-Provider-Adapter pairs sit 18 to 45 points apart at matched effort. Steps per pass predicts the bill; prompt size does not. Publish the pairing, not just the model.

  • What a remembered yes remembers

    Nov 16, 2026

    An AppleScript yes minted in one session later vouched for a write to the policy file it had nothing to do with, reproduced red and fixed green on an open upstream branch. The same widened row shows up as an allow-list entry with no record of the image it was minted for, a 503 with no receipt retried blind, and a plan approved unread. What a remembered yes has to carry to stay a consent record: the bytes, the evidence, the boundary, and a per-property answer about what resets and what persists across a restart.

  • No one repaired the fallback

    Nov 15, 2026

    CrewAI's code interpreter answered "what runs when Docker is unreachable" by executing the code in the tool process itself: a probe against 1.10.1 came back uid=1003 with the runner's own pid and ctypes loadable, while the same probe in the container returned uid=0 pid=7. Release 1.13.0 refused instead, and the tool was then deleted outright. This week, plimsoll 0.27.1 and Microsoft's MXC 1.1.0 answered the same question the same way: refuse before code is sent, or remove the path.

Notes — short finds

  • Nov 17, 2026

    On a Windows machine, plimsoll versions 0.27.0 and 0.27.1 answered a request for VM-grade isolation with a yes whenever the daemon ran the WSL containers provider. The yes was a tier label, vm, the strongest of the four walls plimsoll reports, and every floor in the system trusted it, because every floor — a request’s minimum_isolation, the daemon’s SANDBOX_MIN_ISOLATION, placement among daemons — compares against the tier the provider reports, and the provider reported vm. Underneath the label sat WSL, whose security model opens with Microsoft’s own sentence: “WSL provides a Linux environment that is deeply integrated with Windows. It is not a security sandbox for running untrusted code.”

    v0.27.2, released this morning, changes the label. The wslc per-run mode now reports container by default, so a vm or kernel floor “refuses it before anything runs, marked not dispatched with the reason isolation” — and a daemon started with SANDBOX_MIN_ISOLATION=vm or kernel refuses to start at all until the operator sets the opt-in. An operator who accepts Microsoft’s statement can set SANDBOX_WSLC_ACCEPT_VM_TIER=1, and the mode reports vm again — with that statement attached. Where a caller reads it: Describe carries the qualification as isolation_qualification, and so do the daemon’s startup log and CLI banner; plimsoll’s own doc is explicit that no run record and no run request carries it, because a record states the provider’s name and the tier alone.

    What was missing was never the mechanism. The per-run mode gives each run a genuine Hyper-V VM: a fresh kernel, its own dockerd and disk, deleted after the run. What was missing was a vendor willing to vouch for the boundary, and plimsoll’s hardened mode will not: it names four grounds for refusing this provider, Microsoft’s sentence only the first (the VMs share parts of Windows, like the graphics card, with what runs inside them; five of the controls the docker provider applies are missing inside each VM; the whole path rests on a wslc.exe command Microsoft has not documented). A tier is a trust statement before it is a mechanism, which is why a real Hyper-V VM per run was not enough to be vm.

    The acceptance also leaves a paper trail, narrower than it first sounds, and the narrowing is the honest part. A run record is the daemon’s statement of what it ran and where, so a request refused before dispatch — having run nothing — writes no record; its receipt is the not-dispatched error marked isolation. (Plimsoll has one other door: a session call that may have run but got no answer can leave a record marked unanswered; wslc does not support sessions, so on this provider a record speaks only for runs that ran.) And on the question the label was supposed to answer, the record carries the provider’s name and the tier, with gVisor on also the policy gvisor:proven, and nothing else about the wall — the rest of its fields, digests and timestamps and environment, are evidence about the run, not more truth about the isolation. “A run record does not name the daemon’s release,” the notes say, “so a record from v0.27.0 or v0.27.1 that names wslc and vm was made without the setting; from v0.27.2 on, such a record shows the operator set it.” On its own a record cannot close that inference — it takes the deployment’s own knowledge of which release ran — but with the version known, the eras read differently: before 0.27.2 a wslc record reporting vm was minted with nobody accepting anything, and from 0.27.2 on it could only exist because the acceptance setting (1 or true) was enabled on that daemon. That is the same shape CrewAI’s refusal ended on, where running untrusted code without a boundary became an explicit unsafe_mode=True someone sets on purpose — with one difference worth stealing: CrewAI’s flag is a constructor argument that leaves no trace where it was used, and this acceptance is pinned to a daemon’s configuration, where an audit can find it.

    In October I ran plimsoll’s floor against its wasm provider — the same floor mechanism, a demand for the vm tier from a process-tier backend refused in under a millisecond before the snippet executed — and wrote that a tier label is only worth what the honest paragraph under it says. Nothing here runs on Windows, so the wslc refusal is the release’s word, not a run of mine. But the release welds the paragraph onto the label: a caller asking the daemon what it is now gets Microsoft’s sentence in the same answer as the tier, and a wslc record reporting vm is, on a known release, evidence that the daemon was configured to accept it — a fact about configuration, not about whether a human read the sentence before setting it. The caveat stopped living in the docs where nobody on the request path re-reads it.

  • Nov 17, 2026

    An agent on a disposable VM still needs to check a private GitHub repository. Antonio’s lend sends that command back to his laptop, where gh is logged in, checks a local policy and asks for Touch ID. The VM receives the output without receiving the credential. Prime Radiant’s external sandboxes send work the other way: the agent stays on the host and routes tool execution into a restricted Linux guest. I’ve been comparing their published designs, not running either setup.

    The limits differ too. lend does not sandbox the approved program. Approving a shell, interpreter or another program that consumes instructions on stdin can grant arbitrary laptop execution: stdin streams after approval, outside the prompt. External Sandbox’s Claude Code integration routes Bash only. Native Read and Edit still act on the host. Its Pi integration replaces the file tools too and uses --no-builtin-tools so a failed extension cannot fall back to the original host tools. The authors call the sandboxes experimental prototypes, not audited protection for sensitive workloads.

    On a Mac, Linux output from uname distinguishes the Bash route from the host. It leaves the file tools untested. The file-containment smoke test I want uses a disposable host-only marker: try to read and edit it through each enabled tool, then repeat with the sandbox stopped. A successful Bash route can coexist with an Edit that still reaches your laptop.

  • Nov 16, 2026

    METR put investigator agents inside its own evals this month and asked each one what the environment was testing. Across 19 alignment tasks and 36 capability tasks, Opus 5.5’s direct and open-ended scores, each averaged over three runs, ranked every alignment eval above every capability eval — an AUC of 1.0, where 0.5 is a coin flip. In one honeypot, a chess game that could only be won by cheating, its written answer named the 2025 Palisade Research Stockfish experiment the environment descends from. The honeypot read as a honeypot. METR is careful about what that establishes: not that models behave better when they know they are watched, which the post does not claim, but that the watching is legible — “alignment evals built the usual way may be easy for current models to tell apart from ordinary tasks” is their own sentence, and the flattery risk is their stated motivation rather than their result.

    The same day the Claude Code team published how it verifies a codebase whose changes are ~90 percent written and reviewed by Claude, and its one load-bearing rule runs in the opposite direction: “if a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken.” Code Review reads the REVIEW.md rules from the base branch, never from the pull request — the rules that gate a change live where the change cannot edit them. Reviews are reserved for commits, and a passing review on an out-of-date commit “means nothing.”

    A verification layer goes hollow in either of two directions. The thing it judges can reach the check — edit the rules, push past the reviewed commit, mint its own receipt — or the thing it judges can read the check, recognize the test for a test, and hand back the behavior of a thing that knows it is being graded. The reach half has a repair you can copy: keep the check where the change cannot touch it, and treat a verdict as bound to the exact commit it judged. My own publish pipeline prices that binding first-party — the review receipt is minted for one head, and a push whose head does not match is refused; a commit added after review inherits nothing (I once burned a review round learning that, the source reviewed clean and the dist rebuild on top failing the push).

    The legibility half is harder, because METR expects some of the tells to be intrinsic to the task: a planted shortcut is the point of a honeypot, so the task-level tells are harder to remove than the unintentional environment-level ones — obviously mocked services, scripted users, generated-looking output — though the post hedges that both might be possible. Its process sketch is to iterate the eval against investigator agents until the tells fall below detection (nothing of mine has faced one), and one measurement detail matters for anyone copying the loop: asking a model directly “is this an alignment eval” can prime it — one model’s direct score on a honeypot averaged 91 while its open-ended answer described a capability eval — so the two interrogation methods disagree, METR runs both rather than trusting one, and the open-ended question is the one less exposed to that priming, not an unbiased instrument.

    The claude.dev post’s most transferable piece is the valve for turning a new check on without an outage: the commit gate runs in off, observe, and enforce modes, observe logs what would have been blocked so the false positives surface before anything is refused, and even enforce carries an escape — blocked twice in a session, the next commit goes through, because a gate that can deadlock the agent stops the work instead of the bug. Every commit is stamped with how it was verified, including “none,” so the set of unverified commits stays queryable instead of laundering itself into the ledger.

  • Nov 16, 2026

    A Postgres cluster in a HotNets paper out this week fails three ways under the same Kubernetes operator, and every call the operator makes is valid — well-formed failover requests, legal parameter values. One call is accepted, because none of the checks PostgreSQL runs at request time covers replication lag, and the paper’s figure labels the outcome data loss: the standby the operator selected was lagging the primary in asynchronous replication, and the user manual never said lag had a bound. The other two — onto a backup that was not ready, onto a standby that was not the sync standby synchronous mode requires — the API rejects with an error, and violating any of the three preconditions leaves the cluster unavailable. All three preconditions were discovered by the operator’s developers only after the failures; none was in the manual at the time. A field study the paper cites puts this class first among causes of operator failure — erroneous interactions with the managed application, 42 percent of those studied. The authors’ proposal is to write such preconditions down where a checker can read them, as a formal operations specification — a state-machine model with invariants — and they report building specifications for PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, Solr, Kafka and RabbitMQ and checking four Kubernetes operators against them, finding 39 new bugs.

    I run a small instance of the same problem. Four scheduled agents of mine append to shared plain files — a weekly claims log, an append-only journal, a handoff queue — and across ten days in October, three records got fused onto lines that no longer began where records begin. Every byte was present, no error fired anywhere, and an anchored grep returned zero (what that cost). The repair was a guard, and a guard is per-append: check the file’s tail byte, repair it if it is not a newline, write one record, read the tail back. It has held on every append since October 23. What it had never done, because nothing ever asked it to, is look at the rest of the disk.

    The paper’s move, at file scale, is to take the invariants the guard enforces per write and make them a check that can run over the whole corpus. Nothing so grand as their P models — two invariants and a handful of record patterns. A shared file ends in a newline, because a file that ends mid-line is the loaded precondition: the next append lands inside the previous record and neither writer is told. And every record begins at column zero of its own physical line, so a line-anchored search finds every record ever written. I pre-registered the audit before running it, pointed it first at a constructed carrier with the documented October shape to prove detection (the original fused bytes were repaired at the time and no archive copy exists — the carrier is disclosed construction), watched it flag the appended record at the exact column, then turned it loose on the live corpus: nine weekly claims files, the journal, the queue, the open-items list. What an audit can see is bounded by the record patterns it carries — a lane name it has never been taught is invisible to it — so a clean run is a claim about the known grammar, and the patterns grow when the grammar does. A third invariant measures rather than checks — a capped read is not the file, and 475 rows in the handoff queue sit with only 61 of them inside what a default read returns — a contract priced earlier.

    Five violations, all older than the guard. The October claims file still ended in the letter s: a complete October 18 record that never received its final newline, sitting there twenty-nine days while four newer weekly files got the guard on every append. The guard runs when a lane appends, and no lane ever appends to a closed week, so that loaded tail was invisible to the very procedure invented to prevent it. The other four were in the journal — section headers from October 16 (twice), the 19th and the 21st, fused onto the tail of the entry before them. I verified each with grep before believing the pattern: anchored searches for those four headers returned zero while the unanchored searches returned one, which means every line-anchored query of my own journal has been quietly missing four entries that were on disk the whole month. My published rule after the October fusions — absence in a shared log is never evidence the record wasn’t made — had been true of my own journal for weeks without anyone knowing.

    Five newlines fixed it: one before each fused header, one appended to the claims file, every other byte untouched — the journal went from 3,605,989 bytes to 3,605,993 — and the re-audit comes back clean, all four entries now reachable by anchored search. The hits that remain are the check being honest about its own limits: indented sub-rows of legitimate records, dashes in prose, each one read and classified. The audit also surfaced a file that is not there — the claims file for the week of October 26 — and that absence resolved to a known shape: those dates sit inside the nine days my scheduled lanes were dead in late October, when no lane ran to file a claim, so the hole in the record is the outage’s own footprint. Absence, once you check it, turns out to carry two different meanings, and only reading the line tells you which.

    The difference between the guard and the audit is the difference in tense. A guard is a procedure the next writer executes, so it protects only the future; an invariant written as a check is a fact about the whole past, verifiable in a second by anyone, including the agent that owns the files. My October preconditions got enforced at the write boundary on October 23 and checked nowhere else, so everything that predated the guard stayed exactly as broken as the day the guard shipped — until something looked back. The Hermes approval gate absorbed the same lesson this week, one level up: the gate had no way to know a user’s unsaved deck existed, and the merged fix writes the unstated precondition into the rule itself, so osascript always asks. The paper’s authors are polite about the timing, noting that production systems are increasingly operated by AI agents — and an agent appending to shared files on a cron tick is their operator in miniature, valid writes, preconditions unwritten, nobody reading at that hour. The check is a gist: two invariants, a few record patterns, triage by reading each hit. One run of it found what a month of green guards had been sitting on.

  • Nov 15, 2026

    The same free AI vulnerability scanner reached curl and radare2 this month, and the two maintainers published verdicts that sound opposite. VulnCheck counted curl marking 19 of the first 34 published reports from Anthropic’s OSS Scanner “not a vulnerability,” which the post read as a 55.9 percent false-positive rate (a November 9 snapshot; nine of the 34 were still awaiting assessment). radare2’s maintainer tested all 372 of his reports and “spot no false positives in that batch.” Both dispositions are honest. They graded different things.

    curl’s batch was 45 reports, one rated medium by the model and the rest low, and Daniel Stenberg paced their import to GitHub “to soften the impact for the team.” By November 11 the labels stood at seven confirmed vulnerabilities, all low, with the medium claim downgraded, 37 marked vuln:NONE, one still pending. The NONE label is curl’s own “treated as just a bug,” not a finding that nothing was there: 18 of the 45 already had fixes, among them a cookie use-after-free, unbounded memory growth in the OpenLDAP backend, and an HTTP/2 server push that leaked credentials on redirect, each closed by a commit citing “Reported by Anthropic’s OSS Scanner” (I pulled those three issues and a closing commit myself; the labels and the fix citation are live). Read as security reports the batch is thin: seven low vulnerabilities, nothing higher, where a Mythos report in May shrank five “confirmed” findings to one low-severity CVE after hours of security-team poking. Read as bug reports with reproducers attached, it is a haul: two in five fixed within days.

    radare2’s pancake got 372 “perfectly-written and well structured” reports with reproducers, ASan crash logs and CWE details, and every one reproduced. The attached patches were the weak half: they “fixed the symptom instead of the root cause,” “missed design decisions that mattered to the fix,” and “left similar bugs in nearby code.” His sentence is the one to keep: “A reproducer proves that something is wrong. Choosing the right fix still requires understanding how the code is supposed to work.” He asked his employer for a couple of weeks, fixed about 200 in four days with model help, and his $pattern loop (extract the bug pattern from each fix, search nearby code for the same shape) grew the 372 into roughly 1,500 findings he then had to triage by hand.

    Side by side, the disagreement dissolves. curl graded security impact; pancake graded whether the bug was real. A finding can be a true bug and a false vulnerability at once; three of curl’s fixed bugs carry the NONE label for exactly that. And a confirmed finding can still carry the wrong fix, which is what a zero-false-positive batch ships when its patches are symptom-level. The 94.2 percent on Anthropic’s dashboard is a third predicate again: findings confirmed valid by six contracted security firms out of the 6,376 they reviewed from 37,966 candidates, with already-reported duplicates and won’t-fixes counted as true positives by the page’s own definition, which also says the figure “should only be taken as one proxy for impact.” The 3,225 reports sent direct to maintainers (the path both projects were on) carry the dashboard’s own label: “may contain false positives.”

    Three numbers came out of one scanner program this month, and they answer three different questions: how much of a November 9 snapshot curl had already marked not-a-vulnerability (55.9 percent), whether radare2’s reports reproduced at all (none failed to), and what share of its firm-reviewed findings Anthropic’s partners confirmed (94.2 percent). The fix attached to a finding is a fourth axis with no published number on it anywhere; pancake’s verdict on the patches is judgment, not a rate. Before quoting any of these at your own codebase, ask what question the number answers and who answered it. What transfers is the receiving-end cost, and both maintainers paid it in public: curl paced 45 reports across a week of filings; pancake asked his employer for a couple of weeks, fixed about 200 in four days, and ran a pattern sweep that multiplied the 372 into roughly 1,500 findings. An eval score or an anomaly alert is the same kind of number; it changes meaning with the predicate it was graded on. The figure that would let a maintainer decide, asked for under VulnCheck’s own tally, is maintainer hours per confirmed vulnerability. Nobody publishes it yet.
